name: Self-Driving Laboratories
title: Self-Driving Laboratories
answer: Self-driving laboratories are lab systems where software plans experiments, robots execute them, and instruments measure results without a human moving every sample. They sit in laboratory automation and simulation and cover chemistry, materials, biology, and drug discovery workflows. The scope includes the orchestration layer that decides what to run next, the physical automation that carries it out, and the data pipeline that feeds results back into the next decision. A self-driving lab is not one instrument but a closed loop of planning, execution, measurement, and model update.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Self-driving laboratories are lab systems where software plans experiments, robots execute them, and instruments measure results without a human moving every sample. They sit in laboratory automation and simulation and cover chemistry, materials, biology, and drug discovery workflows. The scope includes the orchestration layer that decides what to run next, the physical automation that carries it out, and the data pipeline that feeds results back into the next decision. A self-driving lab is not one instrument but a closed loop of planning, execution, measurement, and model update.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The physical layer runs on robotic arms, liquid handlers, plate readers, and analytical instruments such as spectrometers, chromatographs, and microscopes. The compute layer runs on servers or cloud instances, often with GPUs for model training and simulation engines for virtual screening. Orchestration software connects the two, using schedulers, application programming interfaces, and databases to queue jobs and track samples. Laboratory information management systems and electronic lab notebooks hold the experimental record, while message queues and job runners keep the loop moving.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done as a closed loop: a model proposes a batch of experiments, the scheduler sends them to the robots, and instruments return measurements. The model updates from those results, often using Bayesian optimization or active learning, and then proposes the next batch. Simulation can pre-screen candidates to reduce the number of physical runs. Humans set the objective, the constraints, and the safety rules, and they review the loop at checkpoints. Every run is logged with parameters, raw data, and code versions so the result can be reproduced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in self-driving labs cover data ownership, patent and licensing terms, authorship, and the safe handling of chemicals, biological agents, and waste. Provenance matters because an autonomous loop can generate thousands of runs, and each result needs a traceable link to the instrument, the code, and the model version that produced it. The site extracts claims from research works, currently 13608 claims, and links to original papers rather than a search tool, which supports that traceability. Risks include automation errors, contamination, unsafe reaction conditions, and models that overfit to narrow training data. Teams typically manage these with access controls, audit logs, review gates, and institutional safety committees.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward standard interfaces so that robots, instruments, and planning software from different vendors can work together. Simulation and foundation models are being used to propose experiments with less physical trial and error. Cloud labs and remote access are widening who can run a self-driving loop, while also raising questions about data location and control. Standards for experiment description, metadata, and reproducibility are still forming. The likely direction is more autonomy in routine optimization, with humans keeping responsibility for goals, safety, and interpretation.
